position: attributive only — *a capital letter*, *a capital crime*
contrast: False friend: Russian *капитальный* (*капитальный ремонт*, *капитальное строительство*) is *major*, *thorough* or *permanent* in English — *a major renovation*, not *a capital renovation*. *The capital* (the main city) and *capital* (money for a business) are nouns.

senses.gloss: Of a letter: in the large form used at the start of a sentence or a name.
examples: Write your name in *capital* letters.
Start every sentence with a *capital* letter.
Is that a *capital* I or a lowercase L?

senses.gloss: Of a crime or punishment: involving the death penalty.
examples: Texas still uses *capital* punishment.
Killing a police officer is a *capital* crime in that state.

position: both — *a capitalist economy*, *The country is capitalist*
contrast: Also a noun: *a capitalist* is a person who owns a business or invests money.

senses.gloss: Based on private ownership of businesses and free markets.
examples: The United States has a *capitalist* economy.
China combines *capitalist* markets with one-party rule.
Is a system really *capitalist* if the government owns the banks?

contrast: *Capitalist* is the neutral, more common word. *Capitalistic* often suggests 'too focused on money and profit'.

senses.gloss: Based on or too focused on private profit and free markets.
senses.ru: капиталистический, погрязший в погоне за прибылью
examples: Critics say the health care system is too *capitalistic*.
He grew up in a *capitalistic* culture that measured success in dollars.
Hong Kong was once called the *most capitalistic* place on earth.

contrast: Russian *капризный* about a child is usually *fussy*, *cranky* or *spoiled* in English. *Capricious* is formal and describes sudden changes with no reason — a boss, a decision, the weather.

senses.gloss: Changing suddenly and without a good reason; unpredictable.
examples: The judge ruled that the firing was arbitrary and *capricious*.
Farmers here depend on *capricious* weather.
The new manager was even *more capricious* than the old one.

position: both — *a captivated audience*, *The audience was captivated*
form: -ed — the person who feels the attraction
contrast: *Captivated* is the person watching; *captivating* is the thing that holds their attention: *a captivating show*, *a captivated audience*.

senses.gloss: So interested or charmed that you cannot stop watching or listening.
examples: The children were *captivated* by the magician.
She watched the dancers with a *captivated* expression.
I've never seen an audience *more captivated*.

senses.gloss: So interesting or attractive that it holds all your attention.
examples: She has a *captivating* smile.
The documentary was absolutely *captivating*.
It was the *most captivating* performance of the night.

ru: пленный, в неволе; вынужденный (о слушателях, покупателях)
position: both — *captive animals*; after a verb mostly in *be held captive*, *take someone captive*
contrast: Also a noun: *The captives were released*.

senses.gloss: Kept as a prisoner or in a cage; not free.
examples: The hostages were held *captive* for three weeks.
*Captive* elephants often live shorter lives than wild ones.

senses.gloss: Of people: unable to leave or to choose something else.
senses.ru: вынужденный, никуда не девающийся (о слушателях, покупателях)
examples: The passengers were a *captive* audience for the pilot's jokes.
Airport restaurants charge high prices because they have a *captive* market.

contrast: Russian *газированный* is not *gassy*: *gassy* means having gas in your stomach. Say *carbonated water* or *sparkling water*; soda that has lost its bubbles is *flat*.

senses.gloss: Of a drink: containing bubbles of gas.
examples: Do you want *carbonated* or still water?
*Carbonated* drinks can be hard on your teeth.
Is this juice *carbonated*?

form: -ic from *carcinogen*, a substance that causes cancer

senses.gloss: Able to cause cancer.
examples: Asbestos is highly *carcinogenic*.
Many chemicals in cigarette smoke are *carcinogenic*.
Researchers are testing which of the two compounds is *more carcinogenic*.

position: attributive only — *cardiac arrest*, not *The arrest was cardiac*
contrast: *Cardiac* is a medical word; everyday speech says *heart*: *a heart attack*, *heart disease*. Russian *сердечный* in the sense 'warm, kind' is *warm* or *heartfelt*, never *cardiac*.

senses.gloss: Of or relating to the heart, especially in medicine.
examples: He went into *cardiac* arrest on the tennis court.
She's a nurse in the *cardiac* unit.
The hospital has one of the best *cardiac* surgery programs in the state.

contrast: False friend: Russian *кардинальный* (*кардинальные изменения*) is *radical*, *fundamental* or *sweeping* — *sweeping changes*, not *cardinal changes*. The noun *cardinal* is a Catholic church official and a red bird.

senses.gloss: Most important; basic.
examples: The *cardinal* rule in this kitchen is to wash your hands.
Lying to your customers is the *cardinal* sin of business.

senses.gloss: Of numbers and directions: basic, as in one, two, three, or north, south, east, west.
examples: One, two and three are *cardinal* numbers; first, second and third are ordinal.
North, south, east and west are the four *cardinal* directions.

contrast: Known mainly from *cardiopulmonary resuscitation*, which everyone calls *CPR*.

senses.gloss: Of or relating to the heart and lungs together.
examples: Every lifeguard must be trained in *cardiopulmonary* resuscitation.
After the surgery he spent six weeks in a *cardiopulmonary* rehab program.
A *cardiopulmonary* bypass machine does the work of the heart and lungs during surgery.

contrast: In gyms the short noun is *cardio*: *I do cardio three times a week*.

senses.gloss: Of or relating to the heart and blood vessels.
examples: *Cardiovascular* disease is the leading cause of death in the US.
Swimming is great *cardiovascular* exercise.
Smoking damages your *cardiovascular* system.

contrast: Not *careless*. *Carefree* is a pleasant state (беззаботный); *careless* is a fault (небрежный, неосторожный).

senses.gloss: Happy and relaxed, without worries or responsibilities.
examples: We spent a *carefree* summer at the lake.
She seemed happy and *carefree*.
I was a lot *more carefree* before I had kids.

contrast: *Caring* is заботливый (kind to others); *careful* is осторожный, аккуратный.

senses.gloss: Kind, and showing that you care about other people.
examples: He's a warm, *caring* father.
The nurses were so *caring*.
She's the *most caring* person I know.

senses.gloss: Formal: relating to the body and sex, rather than the mind or spirit.
examples: The preacher warned against *carnal* desires.
The novel is about *carnal* pleasure and the guilt that follows.
In old legal language, *carnal* knowledge means sex.

senses.gloss: Eating meat.
examples: Lions and wolves are *carnivorous*.
The Venus flytrap is a *carnivorous* plant.
Most sharks are *carnivorous* and hunt fish or seals.

contrast: American *carpet* usually means wall-to-wall carpet (ковролин); a single piece on the floor is *a rug*.

senses.gloss: Covered with carpet.
examples: The bedrooms are *carpeted*, and the kitchen has tile.
We walked down a long *carpeted* hallway.
Is the basement *carpeted*?

position: both — mostly after *get* or *feel*: *I get carsick*
contrast: One word, like *seasick* and *airsick*. The general term is *motion sickness*. Russian *меня укачивает* is *I get carsick*.

senses.gloss: Feeling sick to your stomach from riding in a car.
examples: I always get *carsick* on mountain roads.
Let the *carsick* kid sit in the front seat.
She felt *carsick* after reading in the back seat.

senses.gloss: Cut into a shape or decorated with patterns cut into the surface.
examples: They sat on *carved* wooden chairs.
The front door is beautifully *carved*.
He brought me a *carved* stone bear from Alaska.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb phrase with no hyphens: *We decide case by case*.

senses.gloss: Dealing with each situation separately instead of using one rule for all.
senses.ru: индивидуальный, рассматриваемый в каждом случае отдельно
examples: Refunds are handled on a *case-by-case* basis.
The school takes a *case-by-case* approach to late homework.
The judge made *case-by-case* decisions about bail.

position: attributive only — *a cast-iron skillet*; the noun is written open: *made of cast iron*

senses.gloss: Made of cast iron, a hard iron poured into a mold.
examples: My grandmother cooked everything in a *cast-iron* skillet.
The park still has its old *cast-iron* benches.

senses.gloss: Very strong or certain; impossible to break or doubt.
examples: You need a *cast-iron* stomach to eat that chili.
The suspect had a *cast-iron* alibi.

form: compound — from the phrasal verb *cast off*
contrast: The plural noun *cast-offs* means the things themselves: *I wore my brother's cast-offs*. For clothes Americans also say *hand-me-down*.

senses.gloss: No longer wanted by the first owner and given away or thrown out.
examples: The kids wore *cast-off* clothes from their cousins.
The shelter furnished its rooms with *cast-off* furniture.
He drove his father's *cast-off* pickup truck.

contrast: Russian *случайный* in the sense 'accidental' or 'random' is *accidental*, *random* or *chance*: *a random choice*, *a chance meeting*. *Casual* means relaxed, informal or not serious.

senses.gloss: Relaxed, and not showing much worry or interest.
examples: He tried to sound *casual*, but he was nervous.
She has a very *casual* attitude toward deadlines.

senses.gloss: Of clothes, places or events: informal and suitable for everyday.
examples: The dress code at our office is *casual*.
It's a *casual* restaurant, so jeans are fine.
Can I wear something *more casual* tonight?

senses.gloss: Not regular, close or serious.
examples: We're just *casual* friends.
He's a *casual* fan who only watches the playoffs.
Even a *casual* glance shows the numbers are wrong.

comparison: not gradable — an extreme adjective: *truly cataclysmic*, not *very cataclysmic*

senses.gloss: Causing sudden and enormous destruction or change.
examples: The asteroid had a *cataclysmic* effect on life on earth.
Economists warned of *cataclysmic* consequences if the bank failed.
The flood was *cataclysmic* for the small town.

contrast: Also a noun for the language and the people: *She speaks Catalan*. *Catalonian* exists but is less common. Always a capital *C*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Catalonia, a region of northeastern Spain, or its people or language.
examples: *Catalan* independence is a divisive issue in Spain.
We ate a traditional *Catalan* dish of bread rubbed with tomato.
The architect Antoni Gaudí was *Catalan*.

senses.gloss: Speeding up a chemical reaction.
examples: The car needs a new *catalytic* converter.
Thieves stole the *catalytic* converters from three cars on our street.

senses.gloss: Causing important changes or events to happen.
examples: The protests played a *catalytic* role in the reform.
The grant had a *catalytic* effect on the local economy.

comparison: more/most — *more catastrophic*, *most catastrophic*; with *truly* or *absolutely* rather than *very*
contrast: The stress moves: *catastrophe* is kuh-TAS-truh-fee, *catastrophic* is kat-uh-STRAH-fik.

senses.gloss: Causing terrible damage or suffering; extremely bad.
examples: The hurricane caused *catastrophic* flooding.
A mistake like that could be *catastrophic* for the company.
It was the *most catastrophic* wildfire in the state's history.

senses.gloss: In medicine: unable to move or respond because of a mental illness.
examples: The patient remained *catatonic* for several days.
Doctors treated her *catatonic* symptoms with medication.

senses.gloss: Informal: so shocked, tired or bored that you do not move or react.
examples: After finals week I sat on the couch in a *catatonic* state.
The kids were *catatonic* after six hours of video games.

position: predicative only — before a noun use *contagious* or *infectious*: *a contagious disease*

senses.gloss: Informal: easily passed from one person to another.
examples: Don't worry, this kind of rash isn't *catching*.
Her laughter was *catching*, and soon we were all laughing.
Is the flu *catching* before you have symptoms?

senses.gloss: Of a tune, phrase or name: pleasant and easy to remember.
examples: The song has a really *catchy* chorus.
We need a *catchier* name for the app.
That's the *catchiest* jingle I've ever heard.

contrast: Russian *категоричный* about a person is *uncompromising*, *dogmatic* or *black-and-white* in English. *Categorical* goes with statements: *a categorical denial*, *a categorical no*.

senses.gloss: Of a statement: clear, direct and without any doubt or exception.
examples: The senator issued a *categorical* denial.
The answer was a *categorical* no.
Her refusal couldn't have been *more categorical*.

senses.gloss: Helping you release strong emotions and feel better.
examples: Crying at the funeral was *cathartic*.
Writing the book was a *cathartic* experience for her.
For some people, a hard workout is *more cathartic* than therapy.

senses.gloss: Saying unkind things about other people in a quietly nasty way.
examples: She made a *catty* remark about my dress.
Stop being so *catty*.
The comments got *cattier* as the night went on.

contrast: A trap for Russian speakers: in American forms, police reports and medical records *Caucasian* means 'white', with no link to the Caucasus. A man from Dagestan or Georgia is not called *Caucasian* in everyday American speech; say *from the Caucasus*. Many Americans now simply say *white*.

senses.gloss: White; of European ancestry, used as a formal racial label.
examples: The suspect was described as a *Caucasian* male in his thirties.
The form asks whether you are *Caucasian*, Black, Asian or Hispanic.

senses.gloss: Of or from the Caucasus region between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
examples: The museum has a fine collection of *Caucasian* rugs.
Chechen belongs to the family of Northeast *Caucasian* languages.

position: predicative only — *I got caught up in the story*
takes: *in* + noun (absorbed or involved); *on* + noun (no longer behind with work, reading or episodes)
form: past participle of the phrasal verb *catch up*
contrast: *She caught up with us* is the phrasal verb (догнала). *She was caught up in the scandal* and *I'm caught up on my email* are the adjective.

senses.gloss: So involved in something that you forget other things, or cannot get free of it.
examples: I got so *caught up* in the book that I missed my stop.
He was *caught up* in a bribery scandal.

senses.gloss: Having finished the work, reading or episodes you were behind on.
examples: I'm finally *caught up* on my email.
Don't tell me what happens — I'm not *caught up* yet.

contrast: Do not confuse with *casual* — the same letters in a different order. *Causal* is about cause and effect; *casual* is relaxed or informal.

senses.gloss: Being the cause of something, or showing that one thing causes another.
examples: Scientists found no *causal* link between the vaccine and autism.
Is the relationship *causal*, or is it just a correlation?
The report describes the *causal* chain of events that led to the crash.

senses.gloss: Able to burn or destroy things by chemical action.
examples: Keep *caustic* cleaners away from children.
Lye is extremely *caustic*.

senses.gloss: Of words or humor: very critical and unkind.
examples: She's known for her *caustic* wit.
His reviews got *more caustic* over the years.

senses.gloss: Giving a warning.
examples: His story is a *cautionary* tale about borrowing money.
The doctor added a *cautionary* note about side effects.
The company's collapse serves as a *cautionary* example for startups.

contrast: *Cautious* is about avoiding risk. *Careful* also means doing something with attention to detail: *a careful worker*, *careful work*.

senses.gloss: Careful to avoid danger, risk or mistakes.
examples: Investors are *cautious* about the new market.
She's a very *cautious* driver.
You should be *more cautious* with your passwords.

contrast: False friend: Russian *кавалер* is a noun (a gentleman, a dance partner). The English adjective is negative: not caring enough about something serious.

senses.gloss: Not showing enough care or concern about something important.
examples: He has a *cavalier* attitude toward safety.
The company was *cavalier* about protecting customer data.
I've never met anyone *more cavalier* with other people's money.

senses.gloss: Of a room or space: very large, dark and often empty.
examples: The concert was held in a *cavernous* old warehouse.
The new arena feels *cavernous* when it's half empty.
Their living room was even *more cavernous* than ours.

senses.gloss: Continuing without stopping.
examples: The *ceaseless* noise of the traffic kept me awake.
Her energy seems *ceaseless*.
The nurses worked with *ceaseless* dedication during the pandemic.

senses.gloss: Famous and praised by many people.
examples: She's a *celebrated* jazz pianist.
The chef is *celebrated* for his seafood.
It's one of the *most celebrated* novels of the century.

position: both — *a celebratory dinner*, *The mood was celebratory*

senses.gloss: Done or used to celebrate something.
examples: We had a *celebratory* dinner after the game.
The mood in the office was *celebratory*.
This year's parade felt even *more celebratory* than last year's.

senses.gloss: In or relating to the sky or outer space.
examples: Stars and planets are *celestial* bodies.
Early sailors relied on *celestial* navigation.

senses.gloss: Literary: of heaven; heavenly and very beautiful.
examples: The choir sang with almost *celestial* voices.
The ceiling painting shows *celestial* beings with golden wings.

contrast: American spelling *celiac*; British *coeliac*. Also a noun: *a celiac*, a person with the disease.

senses.gloss: Of or having a disease in which the body cannot digest gluten.
examples: People with *celiac* disease can't eat wheat.
My sister is *celiac*, so we cook without gluten.
The bakery has a *celiac*-safe menu.

senses.gloss: Not having sex, often for religious reasons.
examples: Catholic priests are expected to remain *celibate*.
He lived a *celibate* life as a monk.
She decided to stay *celibate* for a year.

contrast: For phones, everyday American speech shortens it to *cell*: *a cell phone*, *cell service*. British English says *mobile*.

senses.gloss: Of or made of the cells of living things.
examples: The drug works at the *cellular* level.
*Cellular* damage builds up as we age.

senses.gloss: Of mobile phone networks.
examples: The cabin has no *cellular* service.
Our *cellular* data plan costs forty dollars a month.

contrast: Pronounced KEL-tik for the peoples, languages and music, but the Boston Celtics basketball team is SEL-tiks.

senses.gloss: Of the Celts, ancient peoples of Europe, or of the Irish, Scottish, Welsh and Breton cultures and languages.
examples: Irish and Welsh are *Celtic* languages.
The necklace has a *Celtic* knot design.
Most of the music at the festival was *Celtic*.

contrast: Not *censured*, which means officially criticized (осуждённый).

senses.gloss: With parts removed because they are considered offensive, dangerous or secret.
examples: TV stations showed a *censored* version of the movie.
Parts of the report were heavily *censored*.
The *censored* words were replaced with beeps.

contrast: Also a noun: *the town's centennial* (столетие, сотая годовщина). British English prefers *centenary*.

senses.gloss: Marking the 100th anniversary of something.
examples: The city is planning a big *centennial* celebration.
The post office issued a *centennial* stamp.
The university's *centennial* year begins in September.

contrast: American spelling; British *centred*. In compounds it means 'focused on': *child-centered*, *self-centered*. *Centered on* + noun, as in *The talks were centered on trade*, is the verb in the passive.

senses.gloss: Placed in the middle of something.
examples: Make sure the title is *centered* on the page.
The picture on that wall isn't quite *centered*.

senses.gloss: Calm, emotionally balanced and sure of what matters to you.
examples: Yoga helps me feel *centered*.
She seems *more centered* since she changed jobs.

position: both — *central Chicago*, *Family is central to her life*

senses.gloss: In or near the middle of a place.
examples: We stayed at a hotel in *central* Chicago.
I'd rather rent something smaller in a *more central* neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Most important; main.
examples: Family is *central* to her life.
Price was the *central* issue in the negotiations.

senses.gloss: Controlled from one main place for a whole building or organization.
examples: The house has *central* air and heat.
Please send the forms to the *central* office.

contrast: *Central America* is the seven countries from Guatemala and Belize to Panama. Mexico is *North American*, and *Latin American* covers all of Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking America. No hyphen, two capitals.

senses.gloss: Of or from Central America, the land between Mexico and Colombia.
examples: Coffee is a major *Central American* export.
Many *Central American* families have settled in Los Angeles.
Her parents are *Central American* — they came from Honduras.

senses.gloss: Controlled by one central authority or managed from one place.
examples: The Soviet Union had a *centralized* economy.
Hiring is *centralized* at the head office.
The new system is *more centralized* than the old one.

contrast: Also a noun: *a centrist* is a politician or voter in the political center.

senses.gloss: Having political views that are neither left nor right.
examples: She's running as a *centrist* candidate.
His views on taxes are fairly *centrist*.
The party has become *more centrist* over the years.

contrast: The noun *ceramics* means the craft or the objects: *She teaches ceramics*.

senses.gloss: Made of clay that has been baked hard.
examples: We put *ceramic* tile in the bathroom.
She collects *ceramic* bowls from Mexico.
Is this mug *ceramic* or plastic?

position: both — the brain sense only before a noun: *a cerebral hemorrhage*
comparison: more/most — *more cerebral*, *most cerebral*; the brain sense is not gradable
contrast: Also pronounced SAIR-uh-bruhl; both are standard in American English.

senses.gloss: Of or relating to the brain.
examples: He suffered a *cerebral* hemorrhage.
*Cerebral* palsy affects movement and muscle control.

senses.gloss: Using the mind rather than the feelings; intellectual.
examples: It's a *cerebral* thriller with almost no action.
Her new album is *more cerebral* than her earlier hits.

position: both — *a ceremonial sword*; after a verb mostly in the 'no real power' sense: *The role is ceremonial*

senses.gloss: Used in or connected with a ceremony.
examples: The chief wore a *ceremonial* headdress.
The mayor cut the ribbon with a pair of *ceremonial* scissors.

senses.gloss: Having an official title but no real power.
examples: The king's role is largely *ceremonial*.
In Germany the president is mostly a *ceremonial* figure.

contrast: The 'crazy' sense comes from the old legal meaning 'able to be officially declared insane'. It is a joke, not a medical term.

senses.gloss: Informal: crazy.
examples: My neighbor is completely *certifiable*.
Anyone who swims in that lake in January is *certifiable*.

senses.gloss: Able to be officially approved or confirmed.
examples: The farm has to wait three years before its crops are *certifiable* as organic.
Results must be accurate and *certifiable*.

contrast: *Certified mail* in the US is sent with proof that it was delivered (заказное письмо с уведомлением).

senses.gloss: Officially trained and approved to do a job.
examples: She's a *certified* yoga instructor.
All our electricians are licensed and *certified*.
He works as a *certified* public accountant.

senses.gloss: Officially checked and guaranteed as genuine or of good quality.
examples: Send the contract by *certified* mail.
You'll need a *certified* copy of your birth certificate.
We bought a *certified* pre-owned car.

contrast: A medical word. For the neck, everyday speech just says *neck*: *neck pain*, not *cervical pain*.

senses.gloss: Of the cervix, the narrow lower part of the uterus.
examples: Regular Pap tests help prevent *cervical* cancer.
The HPV vaccine protects against most *cervical* cancers.

senses.gloss: Of the neck, especially the bones of the spine in the neck.
examples: He fractured a *cervical* vertebra in the crash.
The doctor ordered an MRI of her *cervical* spine.

contrast: In speech Americans usually say *a C-section*. Also a noun: *She had a cesarean*. British spelling *caesarean*.

senses.gloss: Of a birth: done by cutting through the mother's abdomen.
examples: The doctor recommended a *cesarean* section.
She had a *cesarean* delivery with her second baby.
*Cesarean* births take longer to recover from.

senses.gloss: Of or from Chad, a country in north-central Africa.
examples: N'Djamena is the *Chadian* capital.
*Chadian* troops joined the peacekeeping mission.
Her husband is *Chadian*.

contrast: Formal and literary. In conversation Americans say *embarrassed* or *annoyed*. The *g* is hard and the stress is on the second syllable: shuh-GRIND, rhyming with *pinned*.

senses.gloss: Embarrassed and annoyed, especially because of a mistake or failure.
examples: He was *chagrined* to learn that he had missed the deadline.
She gave a *chagrined* smile when her phone rang during the speech.
I was less *chagrined* than amused by my mistake.

senses.gloss: Like chalk: dry and powdery, or very pale white.
senses.ru: меловой, как мел (о вкусе, текстуре, цвете)
examples: The medicine has a *chalky* taste.
His face went *chalky* white.
This antacid is even *chalkier* than the other brand.

contrast: Americans often use *challenging* as a polite word for *difficult* or even *bad*: *a challenging year*, *a challenging child*.

senses.gloss: Difficult in a way that tests your ability, often in an interesting way.
examples: Teaching middle school is *challenging* but rewarding.
The hike was *more challenging* than we expected.
She wanted a *challenging* job, not an easy one.

senses.gloss: Of a look or question: questioning someone's authority or honesty.
examples: He gave the teacher a *challenging* look.
Reporters asked the mayor some *challenging* questions.

position: attributive only — after a verb say *by chance*: *We met by chance*
contrast: *Chance* is mostly a noun (*a chance to win*, *by chance*). Only before a noun is it an adjective meaning 'accidental': *a chance meeting*.

senses.gloss: Happening by accident, without being planned.
examples: A *chance* meeting at a coffee shop changed her career.
The discovery of penicillin was the result of a *chance* observation.
His *chance* remark started a long argument.

senses.gloss: Informal: risky and uncertain.
examples: Putting all your savings into one stock is a *chancy* move.
The weather in April can be *chancy*.
Driving over the pass got *chancier* after dark.

form: -able from *change*, keeping the *e* so the *g* stays soft

senses.gloss: Likely to change often.
examples: The weather in Denver is very *changeable*.
Teenagers' moods can be *changeable*.
Spring is the *most changeable* season here.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a changed man*

senses.gloss: Different from before, often in an important way.
examples: He came back from the war a *changed* man.
Companies are adjusting to a *changed* world after the pandemic.
The neighborhood looked completely *changed* when I visited last year.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb: *Things are changing*
contrast: In *changing room* and *changing table* the *-ing* word is a noun: a room for changing clothes, a table for changing diapers.

senses.gloss: In the process of becoming different.
examples: Companies must keep up with *changing* technology.
We live in a fast-*changing* world.
*Changing* weather patterns are hurting farmers.

contrast: The *ch* is /k/: kay-AH-tik, as in *chaos* (KAY-ahs).

senses.gloss: Completely confused and without order.
examples: The first day of school is always *chaotic*.
Traffic was *chaotic* after the power outage.
Our house got even *more chaotic* when the twins were born.

senses.gloss: Of skin or lips: dry, rough and cracked, especially from cold or wind.
examples: My lips get *chapped* every winter.
Put some lotion on your *chapped* hands.
His cheeks were red and *chapped* from the wind.

contrast: Russian *характерный* also means 'with a strong personality' (*характерный актёр* is *a character actor*). English *characteristic* only means 'typical'. *A characteristic* (noun) is a feature.

senses.gloss: Typical of a particular person, place or thing.
examples: She answered with her *characteristic* honesty.
This kind of dark humor is *characteristic* of his early films.
Sharp spines are the *most characteristic* feature of this cactus.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun (*a charcoal-gray suit*), usually open after a verb (*The suit is charcoal gray*)
contrast: American spelling *gray*; British *grey*. Often shortened to *charcoal*: *a charcoal sweater*.

senses.gloss: Very dark gray, like the color of charcoal.
examples: He wore a *charcoal-gray* suit to the interview.
We painted the front door *charcoal gray*.
A *charcoal-gray* sky warned of snow.

contrast: *He was charged with robbery* is the verb *charge* in the passive (обвинён), not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Full of strong feelings that could lead to anger or argument.
examples: Immigration is a politically *charged* subject.
The atmosphere in the courtroom was *charged*.
It was the *most charged* debate of the campaign.

senses.gloss: Holding electrical energy, or carrying an electric charge.
examples: Make sure your phone is fully *charged* before the trip.
Electrons are negatively *charged* particles.

position: both — the religious sense mostly before a noun: *a charismatic church*

senses.gloss: Having a strong personal charm that attracts and inspires people.
examples: He's a *charismatic* speaker.
Voters found her warm and *charismatic*.
He's far *more charismatic* in person than on TV.

senses.gloss: Of Christian groups: stressing gifts of the Holy Spirit, such as healing and speaking in tongues.
examples: They belong to a *charismatic* church in Houston.
*Charismatic* services often include loud music and raised hands.

comparison: more/most — *more charitable*, *most charitable*; the 'charity' sense is not gradable

senses.gloss: Relating to giving money or help to people in need.
examples: She works for a *charitable* foundation.
Your donation is a *charitable* gift and is tax-deductible.

senses.gloss: Kind and generous in judging other people.
examples: The *most charitable* explanation is that he simply forgot.
Try to be *more charitable* toward your coworkers.

position: both — the 'lucky' sense only before a noun: *a charmed life*
form: -ed — the person who feels the pleasure
contrast: *Charming* is the person or thing that pleases; *charmed* is the person who is pleased: *a charming host*, *charmed guests*.

senses.gloss: Pleased and delighted by someone or something.
examples: We were *charmed* by the little town.
The guests were *charmed* by her speech.
I was even *more charmed* by her sister.

senses.gloss: Very lucky, as if protected by magic.
examples: She has led a *charmed* life.
It was a *charmed* season for the team.

contrast: Said flatly, *Oh, charming* is sarcastic and means 'how rude' or 'how unpleasant'.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant and attractive.
examples: What a *charming* little house!
Her husband is smart and *charming*.
He was even *more charming* than I'd heard.

contrast: *A charter flight* (noun + noun) is at least as common as *a chartered flight*. *Chartered accountant* is British; Americans say *certified public accountant* or *CPA*.

senses.gloss: Of a plane, bus or boat: hired by a group for a particular trip.
examples: The team flew to Denver on a *chartered* plane.
We took a *chartered* bus to the game.
They went deep-sea fishing on a *chartered* boat.

senses.gloss: Not having sex, or not involving sexual feeling.
examples: Their romance was *chaste* and old-fashioned.
He gave her a *chaste* kiss on the cheek.
The nuns took a vow to remain *chaste*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: liking to talk in a friendly way.
examples: Our Uber driver was very *chatty*.
She gets *chattier* after a glass of wine.

senses.gloss: Of writing or speech: informal and friendly.
examples: She sent me a long, *chatty* email.
The book is written in a *chatty* style.

contrast: In American English *chauvinist* most often means *male chauvinist*, a man who treats women as inferior. Russian *шовинизм* is usually about nationality; English uses *chauvinistic* that way too, but less often.

senses.gloss: Believing that men are better than women, and treating women unfairly.
examples: His *chauvinistic* comments about female engineers got him fired.
Some ads from the 1960s look shockingly *chauvinistic* today.
The *most chauvinistic* jokes came from the manager himself.

senses.gloss: Believing that your own country or group is better than all others.
examples: The speech was full of *chauvinistic* national pride.
*Chauvinistic* nationalism grew in the years before the war.

contrast: *Cheap* often suggests poor quality, so to praise a low price say *inexpensive* or *affordable*. About a person, American *cheap* means 'stingy' (жадный), not дешёвый. *Cheaply* is the adverb, though *buy it cheap* is common in speech.

senses.gloss: Low in price.
examples: Gas is *cheaper* in New Jersey than in New York.
We found a *cheap* flight to Miami.
This is the *cheapest* phone they sell.

senses.gloss: Of poor quality.
examples: The chair broke because it was made of *cheap* plastic.
Her shoes looked *cheap*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: not willing to spend money.
examples: Don't be so *cheap* — leave a real tip.
My uncle is too *cheap* to turn on the heat.

senses.gloss: Unfair or unkind in a way that shows no respect.
examples: Bringing up his divorce was a *cheap* shot.
Jokes about her weight were a *cheap* way to get laughs.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb: *He is cheating*
contrast: In *a cheating scandal* the *-ing* word is a noun (the act of cheating), not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Having a secret sexual relationship with someone other than your partner.
examples: She finally left her *cheating* husband.
The song is about a lying, *cheating* boyfriend.

senses.gloss: Breaking the rules to win or get an advantage.
examples: Fans booed the *cheating* team.
The *cheating* students were suspended for a week.

contrast: Also a noun for the people and the language: *He speaks Chechen*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Chechnya, a republic in the North Caucasus, or its people or language.
examples: Grozny is the *Chechen* capital.
Many *Chechen* refugees settled in Austria and Germany.
Her grandparents were *Chechen*.

position: both — the luggage sense only before a noun: *a checked bag*
form: -ed from *check* (a square pattern; to hand over luggage)
contrast: For patterns Americans more often say *checkered* or *plaid*. The opposite of *checked luggage* is *carry-on luggage*.

senses.gloss: Of cloth: having a pattern of squares in different colors.
examples: She wore a red-and-white *checked* shirt.
The tablecloth in the kitchen is *checked*.

senses.gloss: Of luggage: handed to an airline to carry in the hold of the plane.
examples: Each *checked* bag costs thirty-five dollars.
Put the shampoo in your *checked* luggage.

position: both — the 'mixed history' sense only before a noun: *a checkered past*
form: -ed from *checker*, a square on a checkerboard
contrast: American spelling; British *chequered*. *A checkered past* is not a colorful past but one with scandals or failures in it.

senses.gloss: Having a pattern of squares in two colors, like a checkerboard.
examples: The race ends when the *checkered* flag waves.
The diner has a black-and-white *checkered* floor.

senses.gloss: Having good and bad parts, especially trouble or scandal.
examples: The mayor has a *checkered* past.
The company has a *checkered* history with safety regulators.

contrast: More common in British English. Americans use it for playful, slightly rude behavior; *sassy* is the more American word.

senses.gloss: Slightly rude or disrespectful, often in a funny or charming way.
examples: He gave me a *cheeky* grin.
Don't be *cheeky* with your grandmother.
The *cheekiest* kid in class asked the principal how old she was.

senses.gloss: Happy and positive in the way you look or behave.
examples: She's always *cheerful* in the morning.
The nurse greeted us with a *cheerful* smile.
You seem *more cheerful* today.

senses.gloss: Of a place or color: bright and pleasant.
examples: They painted the kitchen a *cheerful* yellow.
The waiting room was small but *cheerful*.

senses.gloss: Happy and friendly, often in an obvious way.
examples: The waiter gave us a *cheery* hello.
The room felt *cheerier* with the new curtains.
She's annoyingly *cheery* at six in the morning.

contrast: *A cheesy grin* is a wide, forced smile, like the one people make when they say 'cheese' for a photo.

senses.gloss: Tasting of cheese or containing a lot of cheese.
examples: The kids love *cheesy* pasta.
This pizza is *cheesier* than the one we had last week.

senses.gloss: Informal: cheap, silly or too sentimental in an embarrassing way.
examples: He told a *cheesy* joke about accountants.
The movie is really *cheesy*, but I love it.
That was the *cheesiest* pickup line I've ever heard.

position: both — *a chemical reaction*, *The change is chemical, not physical*
contrast: Russian *химический* before a subject or a person is often the noun *chemistry* in English: *a chemistry teacher*, *a chemistry lab*, not *a chemical teacher*. *Chemicals* (noun) are substances.

senses.gloss: Of or produced by chemistry or chemicals.
examples: Rust forms through a *chemical* reaction between iron and oxygen.
The factory was fined for a *chemical* spill.
The difference between the two samples is *chemical*, not physical.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a cherished memory*

senses.gloss: Loved, valued and kept with great care.
examples: The ring is one of her *most cherished* possessions.
I have *cherished* memories of summers at the lake.
Free speech is a *cherished* American value.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun (*a cherry-red car*), usually open after a verb (*The car is cherry red*)
contrast: Russian *вишнёвый* is a dark red, closer to *burgundy* or *dark red*; *cherry-red* is a bright, shiny red.

senses.gloss: Bright red, like a ripe cherry.
examples: He drove a *cherry-red* convertible.
Her lipstick was *cherry red*.
The *cherry-red* barn stood out against the snow.

senses.gloss: Looking sweet and innocent, often with a round face, like a small child or angel.
examples: The baby had a *cherubic* face and big blue eyes.
With his round red cheeks, he looked *cherubic* in his choir robe.
He looks *cherubic*, but he's the class troublemaker.

contrast: *Chestnut* is mainly a noun (the nut or the tree). As a color it is used mostly for hair and horses; for Russian *каштановые волосы* Americans also say *brown* or *auburn* hair.

senses.gloss: Reddish brown, like the color of a chestnut.
examples: She has long *chestnut* hair.
He rode a *chestnut* mare in the parade.
Her hair was *chestnut* when she was young.
